memories.memory_text: I remember standing there on my moped, soaked and shivering, pressing the buzzer under the 'Waste Management' sign, trying to sound steady as I said my name and that I was FBI, transferred from Quantico.

I walked with Professor Broom past glass cases filled with strange artifacts—mummified hands, a clay golem—while he told me how Hitler joined the Thule Society and seized the Spear of Longinus, believing it made him invincible.

After Broom left me at the steel vault door, handing me two Baby Ruth bars, I stood there uncertain as Agent Clay opened the massive door with an electronic key, telling me to come in and meet the rest of the family.

I saw a massive red figure lift a huge dumbbell in the shadows, and when he dropped it with a bang, I flinched—I couldn't help it. Then he spoke, and I realized Hellboy was real, standing right there.

I was told not to stare at his horns, but I couldn't stop myself—I saw the stumps as he stepped into the light, and then he called me out by name. Right after, the alarm went off and he said, 'You're taking me for a walk!'
I opened fire on Sammael’s tongue, rounds tearing into it—amber blood spraying into the air. I didn’t hesitate, even though I’d never done anything like that before.
Hellboy handed me his gun and a fresh clip, then threw me a sealed packet with a single glowing bullet. I cracked the pin and saw the glass head light up like a flare—I’d never seen anything like it.
I called out, voice tight, telling Hellboy he couldn't go without me—I had to go with him. The words came fast, urgent, like if I didn't say them right then, I'd lose the chance.

I was trying to reach Hellboy, asking him to stop and tell me where he was, but then he just said 'Goodbye' and cut the connection—I heard the locator go silent as he walked away into the dark tunnel.

I remember turning toward the door, feeling like I wasn't good enough—like Hellboy would never respect me the way he did Clay—and then Broom said, very quietly, 'I'm dying, Agent Myers.' I froze. His voice was so calm, but it hit me like a shock.

After Abe said I was pure of heart, Broom looked at me and asked me to have the courage to stand by Hellboy’s side after he was gone—to help him become a man, even though he was born a demon. I didn’t know how I could do it, but he was counting on me.
I said I could bring Liz back, that I had experience in hostage negotiations — Hellboy laughed at first, but when I said the words, I saw his expression change.
I told her my name was John, hoping it might make her see me as more than just an agent.
When she said 'Where else would I go?', it stayed with me—like she was trapped, and maybe I was too.
I handed her the Polaroid through the window, said 'Nice view --' and waved. For the first time, she smiled.
I tapped my fingers on the roof of the taxi, keeping time with the music. I couldn't look away from her.
I drew my gun when the locker exploded through the glass wall—glass and metal raining down—and Liz screamed, but then I saw it wasn't a threat, so I holstered it and followed her without a word.
I told Liz what my uncle used to say—that we like people for their qualities but love them for their defects. She didn't answer, just half-smiled and sipped her coffee.
I asked Liz how she felt about Hellboy after telling her he loves her. She said she doesn't know, but admitted he's always on her mind—even now, she said, she feels he's here.
I was trying to say something honest, about how everyone has a hidden side, and I moved my arm behind Liz—then something hit me hard on the head.

I was on the rooftop when Agent Lime suddenly grabbed me—no warning—talking fast, pulling me away while the black B.P.R.D. sedans screeched around the corner. I didn't have time to process what was happening before everything shifted.

I remember the weight of the casket in my hands, the rain soaking through my coat as we carried Professor Broom to the hearse—Manning beside me, the other agents in silent rows, all of us standing witness to something ending.

I saw Liz walk past the conference room while Director Manning was briefing us about the address in Russia—Sebastian Plackba #16, near Volokolamsk—and confirming Hellboy’s involvement, though Manning made it clear he’d be in command.
I used the crowbar to pry open the heavy steel door of the mausoleum, the metal groaning as it gave way.

I turned with my flashlight, and when the light came back on, I saw Sammael—his milky eyes tightening in the glow, crouched among those pulsing eggs, chewing on a bone with flesh still clinging to it. The whole wall was covered in them, like some nightmare hive.

I reached for the explosive belts, trying to arm them fast, but something zipped past—I didn’t even see it move—and then I was on the ground, my clothes torn, the explosives gone. I couldn’t get up in time.
Liz was crying, desperate, telling me to hit her — I stammered, I couldn't do it, I just stood there frozen while the creatures closed in.
I slapped her across the face, hard — then the air rippled with heat and fire erupted from her, forcing me to duck behind a rock as the flames surged outward.
I remember the kick to my face—sudden, brutal—after I shouted not to open the door, and the rosary landing near me, just beyond reach.

I shouted at Hellboy to stop, my voice cracking in desperation as I saw his horns burst forth and that dark energy spreading across the stone—something in me snapped, and I knew I couldn't just stand by anymore.
I lunged forward and struck Ilsa across the face to keep her from taking the rosary—she fell back hard, and I wasn't sure if I'd actually stopped her or not.
I threw the rosary at Hellboy and shouted, 'Remember who you are!'—the words felt like a prayer, and I saw him catch it before the smoke rose from his hand.

Hellboy handed Liz’s body to me and told me to keep her safe, no matter what—he was going to face whatever was back there. I asked if he was going alone, and right after, a huge tentacle came out of the darkness and pulled him away.

I saw Liz's body on the floor, and then Hellboy whispered to her — I couldn't hear the words at first, but when she moaned and opened her eyes, I realized she had come back. I just stood there, watching them, and found myself smiling through tears as the fire rose around them.

memories.memory_text: I was carrying the tray when I heard the patient say there was a big red guy with gold eyes and beer—something inside me froze. I snapped the rubber band hard, wincing, and looked out the window, but the garden was empty.
I found him tangled in that thorny bush again, blood on his arm, trying to play it cool with a six-pack like nothing was wrong — I had to look away before I said too much.
I made the blue flame bloom around my fingers, just enough to see it crawl like a soft haze, and I wasn't afraid—really, for once, I wasn't.
I told him no, that I'm not going back—not this time—and when I said not to come back, I meant it, even if he looked hurt.
I remember saying it on camera—'I don't like the term "firestarter."' It felt stupid, but the words just came out, like I owed someone an explanation.
I looked right at the lens and said, 'With me — it is.' I still see that moment — the silence after, the weight of admitting I could really explode.
I felt his hand on my scar—cold, then burning—and suddenly I couldn't move, like something inside me woke up and started pulling at the dark.
I was just sitting there, and then they started throwing stones—laughing while one hit me in the face. I tasted blood, and I remember it just... dripping onto the concrete.
I felt this heat crawling up my arms, and then I saw the flames—blue and flickering—ringing my skin. I didn’t want it to happen, I was begging it not to, but the fire just came.
I called out for Mommy, my voice breaking—I couldn’t stop it, the fear just ripped through me and everything inside burned.
I was on the steps, screaming—my skin felt like it was peeling off, flames crawling up my arms—and I just kept shouting, 'Mommy! Help me! I'm burning!'
After the light faded, I was still standing—surrounded by rubble and silence—everyone gone, the buildings collapsed, and I was just... a little girl, still crying.
I screamed as the fire ripped through me — I couldn't stop it, I could feel my bones glowing, my skin burning, and then the rubber bands on my wrist were just gone.
I remember the light—my hands wouldn’t stay dark, no matter how hard I tried to pull it back. It was leaking out, past the door, into the hall.

I felt it building again—something hot and wild behind my ribs—and then I saw the flame moving down the hall, like it wasn’t me anymore, like it was its own thing. The glass was shaking, but inside, everything was quiet, too quiet.
I remember sitting on the bench in the padded cell, staring at the camera watching me—like I was some kind of animal behind glass.

He called it a choice—just like that—kneeling there with his hand out, like I was some regular person deciding where to go for coffee. I looked at the mirror, saw us both, and snapped two bands: 'Where else would I go?'
I leaned out of the taxi window, wind in my face, and took a photo—just because I wanted to. For once, it didn’t feel like everything was heavy.
He smiled at me after I handed him the photo, and I actually smiled back. When he said it was a nice view, I wasn’t sure if he meant the city or me—but I took his picture anyway.
I walked in with my suitcases, looked around at all the new glass and brass, and then—crash—the locker came flying through the wall. I said it right then: 'Nothing's changed. Home, sweet home.'
I saw him step through the hole in the wall—just standing there, saying my name like nothing happened. I didn’t say a word. I turned and walked away.
I snapped the rubber band on my wrist—depressed, one snap; impatient, two. It stung, but it kept me grounded after walking back into this fireproof cell they call my room.
I saw the little note in his hand, 'Dear Liz'—he looked like he wanted to say something real, but I couldn’t stay. I asked if it was long, like it was just about time, not about me cutting him off.
I remember laughing with Myers as he handed me my coffee, the cold air sharp in my lungs, the warmth of the cup in my hands feeling almost normal—like I was just someone walking down the street.
Hardly a day goes by he's not in my mind. Even now, I feel he's here — and then I see that red streak jumping over the rooftops, like he’s always lurking just out of sight.
Myers kept defending him — saying he’s determined, strong — and I kept countering with 'pushy,' 'cocky,' 'a brute,' like if I said it enough, it might make it true.
I remember sitting on the bench with Myers, the night air cool against my skin, not knowing Hellboy was watching us from the shadows.
I walked in and saw him there—slumped, so still—and the blood on the floor. I tried not to make a sound, but my breath caught hard, like something tore inside me.
I stood there watching him, then finally said it — I’d go to Moscow. My voice was quiet, but I meant it. I could see he was surprised, maybe even relieved.
He told me he wouldn’t give up on me. Ever. I don’t know what made me say ‘I like that’ — it just came out. It felt true, even if everything inside was still shaking.

I stepped onto that stone, calf-deep in filthy water, and when I shone my light forward—eggs. A wall covered in them. And then I saw him—Sammael—chewing on a bone with a hand still on it. I couldn’t move.

The metal wall slammed up behind us—KLANKKKKK—trapped. Myers tried to set the explosives, but one of them snatched the belts. I grabbed the radio, voice tight: 'Marco, Marco, Marco... Get your Big Red butt over here!'
